ui.title: The first 8 weeks
ui.subtitle: How to support her after the birth
ui.phrases_sub: Sent as a message with one tap.
ui.tasks_sub: Send her what you're taking on so she knows it's handled.
ui.tasks_message: Today I'm taking care of: {list} 💪 You rest.

ui.signs_some: If these signs last more than 2 weeks, see a doctor together.
ui.signs_urgent: You ticked an urgent sign. Don't leave her alone and call emergency services (112) now.
ui.mood_low_title: Her mood has been low lately
ui.mood_low_body: She logged a low mood on {n} of the last 7 days. Give her extra time today and ask how she feels.

ui.disclaimer: This information does not replace medical advice.

weeks.title: The first days at home
weeks.body: After the birth there is bleeding (lochia), and stitches or a caesarean wound hurt. Milk comes in around day 3–5, and her breasts may swell and ache.
weeks.mind: Around day 3–5 hormones drop sharply. Crying for no reason, worry and feeling not good enough are normal: this is the baby blues.
do: Keep visitors to a minimum this week and be the one at the door
Bring water and a snack to every feed
Take over nappies, dressing and bathing the baby
Handle the chores, meals and shopping completely
say: You're a wonderful mum. We're still getting to know each other
If you need to cry, cry. I'm here
weeks.avoid: Don't say "Everyone has babies, what's the big deal?" Don't play down her feelings.

weeks.title: The sleep debt builds up
weeks.body: Bleeding starts to ease. Breastfeeding can still hurt; if there are cracks, a hard lump or redness, see a doctor or a lactation consultant.
weeks.mind: The baby blues usually pass by 2 weeks. If sadness, hopelessness or loss of interest go on beyond that, it may be postnatal depression. Watch closely.
do: Make a night-shift plan so she sleeps at least 4–5 hours in a row
Take the baby out for a walk so she has the home to herself
Find a lactation consultant for feeding questions
Ask "How are you feeling?" every day, and listen
say: Tell me what you need; we'll sort everything out together
weeks.avoid: Don't decide for her or pile on advice. Listen first.

weeks.title: A growth spurt
weeks.body: The baby may want to feed very often (cluster feeding). It doesn't mean there isn't enough milk: the baby is growing.
weeks.mind: Feeding non-stop wears her out and makes her feel she can't keep up with anything. Don't let her feel alone.
do: Sit with her during evening feeds: bring water, food and the remote
Burp the baby after feeds and settle them to sleep
Plan the laundry and cleaning yourself
Cook or order her favourite meal
say: You're growing our baby. It's hard work and you're doing it
weeks.avoid: Don't say "Eating again?" or "Maybe you don't have enough milk". It breaks her confidence.

weeks.title: One month in
weeks.body: Stitches have usually healed, but heavy lifting is still too early, especially after a caesarean.
weeks.mind: Tiredness has built up. She may feel far from her old life, like she is "only a mum" now.
do: Give her 1–2 hours just for herself: a shower, a walk, friends
Plan a small surprise: flowers, her favourite treat, a note
Organise meals and help from family and friends yourself
Make an album of the baby's first photos together
say: What can I do today to make things a bit lighter for you?
I love you so much. Since you became a mum I admire you even more
weeks.avoid: Don't talk about her looks or her weight.

weeks.title: A routine takes shape
weeks.body: Bleeding should be very light by now. If it suddenly gets heavier, or there is a fever or a bad smell, see a doctor.
weeks.mind: A routine is forming, but doing the same things every day can wear her down. If sadness lasts more than 2 weeks, it's time for professional support.
do: Take over one evening routine every day: bath time or bedtime
Plan a short family outing at the weekend
Ask her what's hardest right now and solve one thing
Keep an eye on your own tiredness and talk to her about it
say: Rest tonight, I'll put the baby to bed
weeks.avoid: Don't sum up her day as "you were home all day".

weeks.title: Peak crying and the check-up
weeks.body: The postnatal check-up usually happens around now. Babies cry the most at 6–8 weeks; after that it eases.
weeks.mind: Not being able to soothe the baby is exhausting. When frustration builds, it's fine to lay the baby safely in the cot and breathe for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.
do: Go to the check-up together and write questions down beforehand
Take turns walking the baby during crying spells
Say "I've got this now" and give her a break
Encourage her to tell the doctor how she's feeling, too
say: The crying isn't your fault; babies are like this
Let's take turns, you take a break
weeks.avoid: Don't rush intimacy. She'll tell you when she's ready.

weeks.title: Finding herself again
weeks.body: Her body is still recovering. If the doctor has cleared it, gentle walks and breathing exercises help.
weeks.mind: She's getting to know herself again and may have worries about her body, work or friends. Your support gives her strength.
do: Give her one completely "free hour" each week
Plan a short walk or a café visit together
Keep sharing the night shifts fairly
Say your thanks out loud
say: You're still you, and I choose you every day
You did huge work this month
weeks.avoid: Don't compare: don't say "So-and-so bounced back quickly".

weeks.title: Two months: a new family
weeks.body: Many mums feel stronger by now. If pain, bleeding or exhaustion are still heavy, tell the doctor.
weeks.mind: Her mood should be improving. If sadness, anxiety or feeling distant from the baby continue, talk it through with a doctor together. Help is available and it is treatable.
do: Look back on these two months together: what went well, what should change
Rework how you share the household tasks together
Have a small "two months" celebration
Check your own mood too: dads can have postnatal depression
say: Being parents with you is my greatest happiness
What shall we do differently next month?
weeks.avoid: Don't suddenly scale back your support because "everything's fine now".

blues.title: What are the baby blues?
blues.intro: About 50–80% of women have the baby blues after giving birth. The causes are the sharp drop in hormones, lack of sleep and new responsibility.
facts: It usually starts 2–5 days after the birth
Crying for no reason, irritability, worry and tiredness are common
It usually passes on its own within 2 weeks
The best medicine: sleep, food, support and understanding
help: Listen to her; don't try to "fix" her feelings
Protect her sleep: set up night shifts
Take over the chores and the visitors
Praise her every day and show you're there
blues.ppd_intro: It affects about 10–15% of women and can start any time in the first year after birth. It is not a weakness, and it is treatable.
ppd_signs: Sadness or emptiness lasting more than 2 weeks
She has lost interest in things she used to enjoy
She can't sleep even when the baby sleeps
She feels distant from the baby
blues.ppd_action: If you see these signs, encourage her to see a doctor (her gynaecologist, GP or a psychologist) and go with her.
urgent_signs: Thoughts of harming herself or the baby
Seeing or hearing things that aren't there
Confusion, extreme mood swings, not sleeping for days
blues.urgent_action: In these cases don't leave her alone, and call emergency services (112) immediately.
self: Dads can have postnatal depression too (about 10%)
Take short naps and don't skip meals
Talk about your feelings with her or a friend
Asking for help is a strength

phrases: Whatever you need today, I'm here
Lie down for a bit, I'll look after the baby
I love you so much, you're not alone
You're tired and that's completely normal. We'll manage together
What can I bring you? Tea, food, or just a hug?
Thank you for everything you did today
